key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay minimum-payment option reduced minimum-only credit card payments by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit card debt, with liquidity-constrained cardholders best explaining the null financial effect.
methodology: Field experiment (RCT) on a credit-card autopay enrollment nudge with six-month follow-up.
why_it_matters: Shows in a real, self-directed consumer financial product that changing nominal enrollment via a default-like nudge does not translate into the intended outcome — the clearest direct evidence for the support team's 'enrolment is vanity' worry.
limitations: credit card debt context, not a savings product
the manipulation is a shrouding nudge, not a direct opt-in/opt-out/active-choice comparison
relevance_reason: Closest available consumer-financial field experiment showing enrollment changes need not translate into changed financial outcomes, bearing directly on whether defaults change amount saved or only nominal enrollment.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art narrative synthesis of DC plan design covering short- and long-term effects of automatic enrollment and default investments, including potential negative effects on participant engagement.
methodology: Narrative literature overview, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a recent synthesis of the employer-retirement default literature, including engagement costs, useful background even though it is not about a consumer, self-directed product.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a consumer product
narrative overview with no distinct new estimates in the abstract
relevance_reason: Recent synthesis of the closest large analogous literature (employer DC plans) covering default effects and engagement costs.

key_finding: Argues that default enrollment in US retirement plans raises short-term participation but induces passivity — low contribution rates, inactive management, account churn — undermining long-term welfare claims.
methodology: Narrative policy discussion, abstract-only, no original data reported.
why_it_matters: Restates the general 'defaults create passive, disengaged enrollees' argument but adds no new estimates beyond the stronger empirical papers already in this set.
limitations: employer retirement setting
no original empirical estimates in the abstract
low-tier, uncited venue
relevance_reason: General statement of the passivity/disengagement concern, but redundant with stronger empirical evidence elsewhere in the set.

key_finding: Develops a taxonomy and theoretical framework for how default effects persist or fade downstream, identifying time-course of choice/consumption, antecedent preferences, and trade-off salience as key moderators.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical synthesis and research agenda (Consumer Psychology Review), abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Provides the conceptual framework for exactly the question the brief asks — whether the enrolment default effect persists in depth or amount over time and for whom — useful for designing the 6-12 month measurement plan and distributional analysis.
limitations: theoretical/agenda-setting rather than a specific empirical estimate
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: A recent conceptual review of downstream default effects — the review/synthesis the brief asked for, framed around persistence and heterogeneity.

key_finding: Default rules in Medicare Part D produce large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization for low-income beneficiaries, with passivity remarkably insensitive even to substantial losses from a poor default match, driven by transitory attention shocks rather than stable inattentiveness.
methodology: Three natural experiments with random assignment to default options using Medicare Part D administrative data.
why_it_matters: Strong causal evidence that default persistence can be robust and long-lived rather than a short-run engagement artifact — a caution against assuming disengagement self-corrects, though the setting differs from a consumer savings app.
limitations: government health-insurance program for low-income beneficiaries, not a consumer financial/savings product
no self-directed adult choosing among enrolment designs in a fintech setting
relevance_reason: Closest available large-sample causal evidence on persistence and insensitivity of default effects, useful by analogy though off-domain.

key_finding: Medium- and long-run dynamics shrink automatic enrollment and auto-escalation effects: steady-state savings rates rise by only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation, and only 40% of participants escalate on the first scheduled date, with more opting out over time.
methodology: Longitudinal analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporating job separation, vesting, and opt-out dynamics.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the premise that defaults reliably lift saving in the medium/long run once turnover, withdrawal, and opt-out are accounted for — exactly the support team's objection, with quantified effect sizes.
limitations: 401(k) retirement plans, not liquid consumer savings
abstract-only, no consumer fintech context
relevance_reason: The clearest quantified contradiction of the 'defaults always help' premise, and the closest prior work on medium/long-run attenuation of default effects.

key_finding: Germany's nationwide auto-enrollment of low-income employees into a public pension raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most eligible individuals actively opted out, with a stronger default effect when incentives are high and awareness of enrollment status is low.
methodology: Administrative and survey data analysis of a nationwide public pension auto-enrollment policy in Germany.
why_it_matters: Quantifies a strong default effect size moderated by incentive salience and awareness — relevant heterogeneity evidence, though in a government pension rather than consumer product context.
limitations: government pay-as-you-go pension for low-income employees, not a consumer fintech setting
no data on amount saved or long-run persistence beyond the opt-out decision
relevance_reason: Recent, large-sample quantified default effect with heterogeneity by incentive and knowledge, useful by analogy for the default-effect-size question.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment gains in participation and contributions, replicated at 12 months, attenuate substantially by 36 months, with modest average savings increases at the longer horizon but a significant reduction in savings inequality; a life-cycle model fits this with an estimated switching cost of about $250.
methodology: Analysis of over 100 US retirement plans plus a representative UK panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Directly quantifies the attenuation of default effects between 12 and 36 months, giving a concrete benchmark for what persistence looks like and by how much enrolment gains erode — the exact horizon the brief asks about.
limitations: retirement savings plans (US/UK), not a liquid consumer savings app
switching-cost estimate depends on structural model assumptions
relevance_reason: Closest prior quantified evidence on whether default-driven enrolment gains persist at 12 vs. 36 months, the persistence horizon the brief specifically asks about.

key_finding: Across experiments including a representative five-European-country sample (n=4207), default nudges produced medium-to-large effects on risk-taking but also lowered ratings of the advisor's advice, especially when the default was refused, with perceived honesty mediating the reaction; framing of the default question produced smaller additional effects.
methodology: Three experiments, including a large representative multi-country European sample, on default framing in financial risk-taking decisions.
why_it_matters: Gives direct EU consumer evidence that a financial default can backfire on trust/perceived honesty when overridden or refused — informing when a round-up default reads as helpful versus manipulative, the dark-pattern risk the brief flags.
limitations: setting is investment/wealth-management advice with an advisor present, not a fully self-directed app
no reported 6-12 month retention outcomes
relevance_reason: The only paper in the set giving direct EU consumer evidence on when a financial default is perceived as manipulative, bearing on reputational/dark-pattern risk.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment raised 401(k) participation above 85% at three firms, but roughly 80% of participants initially accepted the default 2-3% savings rate and default conservative fund, with half still at the default rate/fund after three years, so higher participation and low anchoring roughly offset in the lower tail of savings.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms' 401(k) plans.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that a preset level anchors most enrollees for years — the necessary foundational result behind the anchoring concern the brief raises about which round-up multiplier to pre-select.
limitations: employer 401(k) retirement plans, not a consumer savings app
predates recent fintech/app contexts and the EU regulatory climate
relevance_reason: The foundational study establishing that preset default levels anchor participant choices for years, the necessary precedent for the pre-set-level anchoring question.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of deviation cost and opt-out effort cost together, and that adding an intermediate tip option below the existing menu captures 69% of the achievable welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6 million tipping transactions plus a stated-preference survey.
why_it_matters: Offers a transferable method for decomposing why a preset level anchors choices — preference-deviation cost versus opt-out-effort cost — useful for deciding whether an intermediate round-up multiplier option would capture most welfare gain without eliminating the blank-field choice.
limitations: tipping decisions, not a savings/financial-commitment context
no data on persistence or amount saved over time
relevance_reason: Provides a structural method for decomposing why preset default levels anchor choices, transferable to deciding whether/how to preset the round-up multiplier menu.

key_finding: An opt-in short-term, liquid, withdrawable-anytime payroll savings program at five UK firms had very low take-up (at most 0.7% of eligible employees ever activated an account) but strong 12-month persistence among adopters (96% retained a positive balance, 87% received a contribution at month 12).
methodology: Field study of a short-term savings account rollout at five UK employers, tracking activation and 12-month account activity.
why_it_matters: The closest available evidence on the specific opt-in trade-off the brief is deciding: an opt-in liquid savings product gets very low enrolment but the people who opt in stay highly engaged for a year — directly bears on whether opt-in alone would leave enrolment too low despite good engagement quality.
limitations: employer payroll-deduction delivery, not a direct-to-consumer banking app
no comparison arm with opt-out or active choice
relevance_reason: Directly measures the opt-in take-up/persistence trade-off for a short-term liquid savings product, the closest product analog to round-up savings in the shortlist.

key_finding: Characterizes when opt-out minimization versus maximization is asymptotically optimal in a general default-design model, showing that when designer and choosers agree on the activity's value, weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions to externalities, fees, and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/computational model with asymptotic characterization and numerical simulations, abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a general normative theory of when defaulting people in is welfare-optimal versus not, useful background for reasoning about the welfare trade-offs of an opt-out design, though abstract and not tied to a specific financial product.
limitations: fully theoretical/abstract, no empirical estimate for any consumer product
does not address persistence, anchoring at a specific level, or active choice directly
relevance_reason: General theoretical framework for when opt-out defaults are welfare-optimal, useful background for the ethics/welfare side of the opt-out decision.

key_finding: Maps EU law's treatment of dark patterns (pre-selected defaults among them) onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, showing EU regulation targets protection of biased consumers' autonomy.
methodology: Doctrinal legal analysis and taxonomy-building; abstract-only for empirical content.
why_it_matters: Directly informs whether an opt-out enrollment design risks being read as a regulated dark pattern in the EU, which is the reputational/legal constraint the brief flags explicitly.
limitations: legal/normative analysis, not empirical evidence on enrolment or amounts saved
no financial-product-specific case studies
relevance_reason: Only paper in the set giving an EU-specific framework for when a default is manipulative versus acceptable, directly bearing on the entry-decision's legal risk.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs ~50% at lower defaults), and default-anchored contributors had systematically lower incomes than predicted, indicating strong anchoring especially among lower-income employees.
methodology: Administrative retirement-plan data, comparison against literature-review benchmark of lower-default opt-out rates.
why_it_matters: Strong evidence that preset contribution levels anchor the chosen level rather than being freely adjusted, directly bearing on whether to pre-set a round-up multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a self-directed consumer app
no employer-as-intermediary control for our setting
relevance_reason: Closest available quantification of anchoring on a preset contribution level, though in an employer-pension setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/unavailable ('Trant'), so no extractable findings on the four large U.K. payroll-savings experiments.
methodology: abstract-only; content not retrievable from the provided text.
why_it_matters: Title and authorship (Beshears/Choi/Laibson) suggest direct relevance to automated short-term liquid savings, but no usable evidence can be drawn from what is given.
limitations: abstract is unusable/corrupted
cannot verify claimed effect sizes or setting details
relevance_reason: Potentially highly relevant to short-term automated savings but currently unscorable beyond title-level relevance.

key_finding: Automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts at UK banks reduced unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, worth an estimated £170-240 million market-wide, though alerts captured less than half of potential savings.
methodology: At-scale field experiments run by major U.K. banks (RCT-style rollout).
why_it_matters: The closest real analog we have: an opt-out (automatic enrollment) consumer-banking-app feature with measured financial outcomes, giving a benchmark effect size and showing defaults only partially close the potential-savings gap.
limitations: outcome is charge avoidance via alerts, not a savings-pot product
does not report multi-year retention or disengagement specifically
relevance_reason: Directly analogous consumer-banking opt-out feature with quantified benefit, the strongest same-setting evidence in the shortlist.

key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised savings by £32-38/month but also raised unsecured debt by £7/month and mortgage balances, showing partial offsetting of nominal savings gains.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from randomized roll-out of UK automatic enrollment across ~160,000 small employers.
why_it_matters: Evidence that a headline enrollment/savings increase can be partially illusory once offsetting borrowing is accounted for — relevant to the 'amount saved vs nominal enrollment' question, though in a pension not liquid-savings context.
limitations: employer pension, not a consumer app feature
debt offset mechanism may not transfer to small round-up sums
relevance_reason: Best available evidence that default-driven savings increases can be partially offset elsewhere in household finances.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' to health insurance auto-enrollment reduced enrollment by 33%, disproportionately excluding young, healthy, and disadvantaged people.
methodology: Quasi-experimental analysis of removal/addition of an ordeal step in auto-enrollment, with a selection-market model.
why_it_matters: Shows that adding friction (analogous to active choice or opt-in) can produce large, distributionally uneven exclusion — a caution for assuming active choice is a costless middle ground.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not consumer savings
adverse-selection framing doesn't map directly onto a savings feature
relevance_reason: Strong distributional evidence on who is excluded by added friction, relevant to the active-choice-vs-default trade-off in a different market.

key_finding: Pre-checked recurring-donation defaults on political campaign websites raised donations by over $43 million but also increased requested refunds by almost $3 million, with larger effects on smaller and less-experienced donors who did not compensate by changing donation amounts.
methodology: Staggered difference-in-differences design across campaign websites around the 2020 U.S. election.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the support team's concern: an opt-out-style default on a recurring financial commitment lifts nominal sign-ups but generates disproportionate regret/refunds among smaller, less experienced users — a real-money analog to complaint risk from passive enrollment.
limitations: political donations, not a savings product
no data on long-term retention beyond refund requests
relevance_reason: The clearest real-world evidence that recurring-financial defaults produce measurable manipulation/regret costs concentrated on the least-experienced users, directly bearing on the enrollment-vs-engagement trade-off.

key_finding: In a search model with a default option, defaults raise reservation utility via a reference effect, and higher-reservation-utility individuals self-select into active search and find better options.
methodology: Lab experiment testing a reference-dependent search-with-default theoretical model.
why_it_matters: Offers a general behavioral mechanism for why some users reject defaults to find better options, but not tied to a financial product or consumer-app setting.
limitations: abstract lab task, not a financial or app context
no measure of enrollment, retention, or amount saved
relevance_reason: General mechanism evidence on default/search behavior, only loosely applicable to the specific decisions at hand.

key_finding: Following the EU Digital Markets Act's mandated active-choice browser screens, Firefox usage was 113% higher on iOS and 12% higher on Android 15 months after rollout relative to a no-mandate counterfactual.
methodology: Difference-in-differences design exploiting staggered DMA rollout across iOS and Android.
why_it_matters: Direct, large-scale, persistent (15-month) evidence that mandated active choice can meaningfully shift behavior away from an incumbent default in a mobile consumer app under EU regulation — the closest available evidence on whether active choice captures real behavioral change rather than token compliance.
limitations: outcome is browser choice, not financial enrollment or savings amount
platform-specific rollout differences complicate generalization
relevance_reason: The strongest available active-choice-vs-default comparison in a mobile app, EU-regulatory setting, directly informing the active-choice option under consideration.

key_finding: In a 410-participant usability study, generalizable active opt-out privacy choice schemes reduced disruption (98% not feeling disrupted for the least disruptive scheme, a 40-point increase over baseline) at a slight cost to opt-out utility.
methodology: Design and usability study of nine privacy-choice interface schemes in a browser extension, legally motivated by no-default-allowed opt-out requirements.
why_it_matters: Offers a concrete design pattern for making a no-default active-choice interface low-friction, relevant if active choice is chosen for onboarding rather than an opt-out default.
limitations: privacy opt-out setting, not financial enrollment
no measure of downstream financial behavior
relevance_reason: Useful design precedent for building low-friction active choice without defaults, though outside the financial-product setting.

key_finding: Opt-out defaults for university exam sign-up increased task uptake, but increased effortful completion only for individuals previously responsive to university communication; non-responsive individuals saw sign-up gains with no effect on actual completion.
methodology: Two field experiments changing sign-up defaults for exams in two study programs.
why_it_matters: Directly supports the support team's worry that passively enrolled, less-engaged users show nominal sign-up gains without real behavior change — heterogeneity by responsiveness type.
limitations: university exam context, not financial savings
small number of programs studied
relevance_reason: Clear heterogeneity evidence that defaults can inflate nominal participation without moving effortful outcomes for less-engaged users.

key_finding: After target-date funds became the default option under the Pension Protection Act, younger and older workers' stock allocations shifted in line with the TDF glidepath, but contribution rates changed little.
methodology: Account-level panel data on millions of U.S. investors, 2006-2018, exploiting the PPA policy change.
why_it_matters: Shows that a preset default can strongly anchor which option is selected (glidepath allocation) while leaving the underlying contribution/commitment level largely unaffected — relevant to whether a preset multiplier would anchor round-up level choice.
limitations: employer retirement plan, not consumer app
measures asset allocation default, not enrollment or contribution-level default directly
relevance_reason: Evidence that presets anchor the specific option chosen without necessarily changing overall commitment, informative for the multiplier-preset decision.

key_finding: In a 220-participant RCT on voluntary pension saving in China, default-option nudges (along with other nudges) significantly reduced willingness to contribute and contribution share relative to a control group, with heterogeneity by income, education, and gender.
methodology: Randomized controlled trial via online survey testing social-norm, framing, and default-option nudges.
why_it_matters: Directly contradicts the brief's working premise that 'defaults will lift enrolment' — evidence that a default can backfire and reduce contribution willingness, which the internal debate needs to weigh against the assumption defaults are safe.
limitations: small online-survey RCT (n=220), not a live financial product
Chinese cultural/institutional context may not generalize to EU consumer app users
relevance_reason: The clearest contradicting evidence in the set that defaults can backfire on willingness to save, directly answering the brief's request for a paper against the 'defaults always help' premise.

key_finding: In a pre-registered survey of 2,100 Australians, financial nudges were rated positively overall, with stronger approval for System-2 (reflective) interventions and savings-framed messages, while transparency had no significant effect on approval.
methodology: Pre-registered online survey experiment with 36 hypothetical financial-intervention vignettes varying transparency, framing, and System-1/2 targeting; representative Australian sample (n=2,100).
why_it_matters: Speaks directly to the reputational/dark-pattern risk named in the brief: people generally approve of financial nudges, and framing/reflectiveness (not disclosure) drives approval — evidence for how to frame the round-up default so it reads as helpful rather than manipulative.
limitations: Hypothetical vignette survey, not an actual product enrollment decision
does not test round-up savings specifically
no measure of actual enrollment or amount saved
relevance_reason: Directly tests when financial nudges/defaults are perceived as manipulative vs helpful — the EU dark-pattern risk the brief flags.

key_finding: Offering CCT beneficiaries the choice of bank-account deposit over cash produced no significant average effect on savings, but raised balances specifically among those with no prior savings.
methodology: Field experiment among conditional-cash-transfer beneficiaries comparing cash vs. bank-account delivery; abstract-only detail on scale.
why_it_matters: Illustrates that account-based delivery methods can shift savings for the least-prepared but do little for typical enrollees, a minor cross-check on distributional effects but not on enrollment defaults.
limitations: Developing-country cash-transfer recipients, not a consumer banking-app population
delivery-method choice, not an enrollment-default manipulation
abstract omits effect sizes
relevance_reason: Adjacent evidence on heterogeneous savings-behavior effects of account-based delivery, useful mainly as a distributional cross-check.

key_finding: Compares automatic-IRA account designs with and without an emergency-savings component on liquid-fund balances; abstract text is fragmentary and gives no extractable comparative result.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to compare account variants in a universal automatic IRA program.
why_it_matters: Emergency/liquid-savings design inside an automatic-enrollment account is conceptually close to the round-up pot, but the abstract gives nothing actionable.
limitations: Abstract too fragmentary to extract findings or effect sizes
retirement-account (IRA) context rather than a bank app
national auto-IRA program, not a consumer product decision
relevance_reason: Nominally about emergency/liquid savings inside an automatic-enrollment retirement vehicle, but too thin to inform the decision.

key_finding: Switching a 401(k) plan from opt-in to automatic enrollment dramatically raised participation, and most automatically-enrolled employees stuck to both the default contribution rate and default fund allocation even though almost no one had chosen that combination under opt-in.
methodology: Before/after administrative-data comparison of one large US corporation's 401(k) plan around an automatic-enrollment policy change.
why_it_matters: The classic demonstration that default participation carries over into anchoring on the specific default level — the direct precedent behind the worry that a pre-set multiplier will anchor round-up levels, but via an employer-mediated mechanism the brief says doesn't transfer.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k), not a consumer app the user chooses for themselves
2001 data, predates current fintech/regulatory context
single-firm case study
relevance_reason: Foundational, closest-in-spirit prior evidence for anchoring on preset default levels, but off-domain (employer retirement) so capped.

key_finding: Compares savings behaviors between automatically-enrolled and voluntarily-enrolled defined-contribution retirement-plan participants; no abstract text available to state a specific result.
methodology: abstract-only; appears to be an observational comparison of enrollment types in a DC retirement plan.
why_it_matters: Potentially another auto-enrollment-vs-voluntary comparison, but with no abstract there is nothing to weigh against stronger evidence already in this set.
limitations: No abstract available
employer/plan retirement context, not consumer product
cannot assess effect size or recency of design
relevance_reason: Title suggests direct relevance to opt-in vs opt-out enrollment, but lack of abstract prevents extracting usable evidence.

key_finding: Low institutional trust and minority/non-national status are associated with both under-saving and early withdrawal from a mandatory pension scheme, across three representative Estonian surveys (2020-2022) around a policy reform.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of three nationally representative Estonian surveys around a pension early-withdrawal reform.
why_it_matters: Evidences the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' concern: the same low-trust population most likely to disengage is also most likely to withdraw early, mapping onto the support team's disengagement worry.
limitations: Mandatory pension savings context in Estonia, not a voluntary consumer app
correlational survey design, no causal identification of a default's effect
early-withdrawal decision differs structurally from disabling a round-up feature
relevance_reason: Distributional evidence that the population most likely to be passively enrolled is also most likely to withdraw early — supports the support team's disengagement concern.

key_finding: In a 24,303-respondent G7 survey experiment, prompting people to reflect on a default-enrollment vaccine-booster policy reduced their stated intention to get boosted and reduced approval of the automatic-enrollment policy itself.
methodology: Large-scale online survey experiment (n=24,303) across G7 countries manipulating reflection on a hypothetical default-enrollment policy.
why_it_matters: Contradicts the assumption that defaults are uniformly well received once noticed; a warning that surfacing the round-up default too prominently could backfire, echoing the dark-pattern risk in the brief.
limitations: Vaccination policy domain, not a financial product
hypothetical policy vignette rather than actual enrollment
backlash mechanism may not generalize to a low-stakes savings feature
relevance_reason: Contradicts the assumption that default enrollment is uniformly well received once people notice it, relevant to the manipulation/dark-pattern risk named in the brief.

key_finding: Among US millennials surveyed in 2018, automatic enrollment and employer matching contributions were both associated with higher retirement-plan participation, while their absence was linked to non-participation.
methodology: Cross-sectional analysis of the 2018 FINRA Millennial Investment Study survey data.
why_it_matters: Confirms the standard default-participation finding in a younger cohort but adds little beyond the 401(k) literature already covered by stronger evidence in this set.
limitations: Employer-sponsored retirement plans, not a self-directed consumer app
correlational survey with no causal identification of the default's own effect apart from matching
no data on amount saved, persistence, or anchoring
relevance_reason: A recent but largely confirmatory employer-plan enrollment study that duplicates findings already covered by stronger evidence in this set.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish savings records, automatic employer contributions substantially raised total wealth accumulation, while subsidies requiring active choice induced only about 1 cent of extra saving per dollar of subsidy, because roughly 85% of individuals are 'passive savers' unresponsive to subsidies but moved by automatic contributions.
methodology: Population-scale administrative panel data from Denmark exploiting variation in subsidy and automatic-contribution policies; decomposes 'active' vs 'passive' saver responses.
why_it_matters: The strongest available evidence that defaults change actual savings amounts, not just nominal enrollment, and that most people don't respond to elective incentives — a central input to whether enrollment should default users in versus rely on active-choice prompts.
limitations: Danish retirement-savings accounts, not a liquid consumer banking app
government subsidy vs. automatic employer contribution, not opt-in/opt-out/active-choice as this brief defines them
does not test active choice as a distinct enrollment mechanism
relevance_reason: Population-scale causal evidence that passive defaults move actual saved amounts while active elective incentives barely do — directly answers the brief's 'amount saved vs. nominal enrollment' question.

key_finding: Field experiments show 'active choice' (requiring a yes/no decision with no default) increases engagement, and an 'enhanced active choice' variant that highlights losses from the non-preferred option can approach the effectiveness of automatic enrollment where opt-out defaults are infeasible.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments testing active choice and a novel 'enhanced active choice' design, building on the Carroll/Choi/Laibson/Madrian/Metrick active-choice literature from savings research.
why_it_matters: The direct precedent for the third entry option the brief is weighing — active/forced choice — and for whether a modified active-choice design can recover most of the opt-out enrollment benefit without the disengagement risk; explicitly recommended as a complement when automatic enrollment is undesirable.
limitations: Field experiments are in medication-adherence/health settings, not a financial app
no data on downstream amount saved or persistence over months
the 'enhanced' variant nudges toward one option, raising its own manipulation-risk question
relevance_reason: The founding empirical test of 'active choice' as an alternative to opt-out defaults — precisely the third entry-mechanism the brief is deciding among.

key_finding: A broad review of household-finance behavior finds classical-model-inconsistent patterns across saving, borrowing, payments, asset allocation and insurance, and surveys interventions — including choice architecture and product design — that firms and governments use to shape those outcomes.
methodology: Narrative review/book chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and behavioral-economics explanations plus a survey of intervention types.
why_it_matters: The only broad synthesis in this set spanning consumer financial behavior generally (not just retirement) and choice-architecture interventions, giving the review-level context the brief asked for.
limitations: Narrative overview, not a systematic review or meta-analysis with pooled effect sizes
abstract does not itself state numeric default-effect estimates
retirement savings still receives outsized emphasis relative to consumer fintech products
relevance_reason: The most relevant available review-level synthesis of choice-architecture effects across household finance, satisfying the brief's ask for a review or meta-analysis rather than a single study.

key_finding: Across three large firms, automatic 401(k) enrollment pushed participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted both the low default contribution rate and conservative default fund, and half were still at the default rate and fund after three years.
methodology: Multi-year administrative-data analysis of automatic-enrollment 401(k) programs at three large US firms.
why_it_matters: Gives the clearest quantified precedent for the anchoring worry — a preset default level doesn't just get accepted at signup, it persists for years — directly informing whether a pre-selected round-up multiplier will anchor most users long-term, and shows the participation-vs-amount tradeoff.
limitations: Employer-sponsored 401(k) plans, not a self-directed consumer savings feature
2001-era data predating current fintech/regulatory norms
does not test active choice as a third option
relevance_reason: The strongest available long-horizon (3-year) evidence that a preset default level anchors contribution choices and offsets participation gains — the closest prior work on the Level decision.

key_finding: Randomly assigning Afghan employees to different salary-linked savings-account default configurations raised participation by 40 percentage points — equivalent to a 50% matching incentive — driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating scenarios, and default assignment also increased later active saving decisions.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with multiple treatment arms varying default account features, plus follow-up measurement of post-study active saving decisions.
why_it_matters: The clearest causal evidence on why defaults work — cognitive cost and present bias rather than employer trust — which bears directly on whether an active-choice prompt can recover the enrollment benefit without defaulting people in.
limitations: Salary-linked accounts for employees in Afghanistan, a very different population and regulatory context from an EU consumer banking app
mechanism decomposition is specific to a low-financial-inclusion setting
does not directly test a round-up multiplier or active-choice enrollment design
relevance_reason: The strongest causal (RCT) evidence for the mechanism behind default effects — cognitive cost and present bias — which is exactly what active choice is meant to address, bearing directly on whether active choice can substitute for opt-out.

key_finding: Payment reminders cut late-payment fees by 14% overall but raised overdraft fees by 9% for users with an overdraft history, leaving that subgroup with a 5% net increase in fees while others saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil; abstract-only for further design detail.
why_it_matters: Directly demonstrates that a well-intentioned nudge in a consumer fintech setting can help most users while quietly harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the distributional risk the brief asks us to check before defaulting everyone into round-up savings.
limitations: studies reminders, not enrolment defaults or preset contribution levels
